title: Neverland Navigation: Maps, Scale, and Time
topic: Maps, scale, latitude and time, and proportional thinking through Peter Pan
lens: Peter Pan by J. M. Barrie (1911)
description: Peter can fly but you cannot, so you need a map that is true. Follow Barrie's Neverland as a mapmaker's problem: scale a sketch, find position with latitude, and plan time across space. Ratios carry every page. Inspired by a book and play in the public domain in the United States. All illustrations are original.
author: Well of Wisdom contributors

lessons.title: Scale: small drawing, real island
lessons.summary: A drawing distance becomes a ground distance through the scale.

content.title: How big is Neverland on paper?
content.body:
Wendy looks at Nana's old sketch of Neverland and wonders how far the lagoon is from the hill. The sketch says $1\ cm : 2\ km$, one centimetre on paper stands for two kilometres on the ground. The lagoon to the hill measures $6\ cm$ along the path.

- **Scale** multiplies map length into ground length: $ground = map \times scale$
- Measure **along the path**, not in a straight jump between endpoints
- Keep units matched: centimetres on the map times kilometres per centimetre
- A larger scale number means each map centimetre stands for more ground

$6 \times 2 = 12\ km$ from lagoon to hill. Peter could fly it. You would walk it.

content.prompt: On a map where 1 cm = 3 km, a trail measures 7 cm along its curves. How many km on the ground?
content.hint: Multiply the map centimetres by km per centimetre.

content.prompt: Which scale stands for more ground per centimetre on the map?
content.explanation: Each centimetre on the first map represents ten km, more than two.
content.hint: Which number after the colon is larger?

lessons.title: Latitude and the sea around the map
lessons.summary: Lines that run sideways tell how far north or south you are.

content.title: Where is Neverland on the world?
content.body:
Barrie says Neverland is second to the right and straight on till morning, which is not a real direction. Real sailors use **latitude**, the lines that run east and west, measured in degrees north or south of the equator. Longitude runs north to south and meets them in a grid. The pair names a place.

- **Latitude** runs sideways like steps around the globe. 0 at the equator, 90 at the pole.
- **Equator** splits north and south. The Tropic of Cancer lies near $23.5^\circ$ N.
- Moving north increases latitude north. Moving south past the equator increases latitude south.
- Latitude alone is not enough to name a spot. You need longitude too, the other line of the grid.

content.prompt: Which line tells how far north or south a place is from the equator?
content.explanation: Latitude measures north-south position in degrees from the equator.
content.hint: Which word matches sideways lines around the globe?

content.prompt: A point lies at 10 degrees N, then sails west along that line of latitude. What changes and what stays the same?

choices.text: Latitude stays at 10 N, longitude changes
The place is no longer at sea

content.explanation: Sailing along a latitude line keeps latitude fixed and changes longitude.
content.hint: Does sailing along a sideways line change your distance from the equator?

lessons.title: Direction on a real map
lessons.summary: A compass rose and a path that bends.

content.title: Wendy checks the rose
content.body:
The sketch has a compass rose with **north, east, south, west** and the halves near the corners: northeast, southeast, southwest, northwest. John says the hill is southeast of the lagoon. Wendy turns until the rose's north points the way her feet expect, then sees he is right.

- On a printed map, north is usually at the top unless the arrow says otherwise
- The rose's **arrow** tells north. Assume nothing if there is no arrow.
- Between north and east lies northeast, exactly halfway

content.prompt: On a standard map with no special arrow, which way is north?

choices.text: Toward the top of the page
Toward the bottom of the page

content.explanation: Standard orientation places north at the top. A special north arrow overrides that if present.
content.hint: Where does a standard map put north?

content.prompt: John is at the lagoon and the hill is southeast of him. To face the hill, in which general compass octant does he turn?
content.explanation: Southeast lies halfway between south and east.

lessons.title: Speed as a ratio: distance for time
lessons.summary: Speed ties distance and time in one ratio, $speed = distance / time$.

content.title: Peter's pace, your pace
content.body:
Peter says he flew from the nursery to the second star in moments, which is not a measurement. Wendy times herself along the beach: $12\ km$ in $3\ hours$. Her average **speed** is $distance / time$.

- $speed = distance / time$. Units like $km/h$
- Then $distance = speed \times time$ and $time = distance / speed$
- Average speed hides rests and hills. It is still the tie that lets you plan

$12 / 3 = 4\ km/h$ along the sand. The hill path will be slower, so do not use the beach number for a mountain.

content.prompt: Wendy walks 18 km in 3 hours. What is her average speed in km per hour?
content.explanation: 18 divided by 3 equals 6 km per hour.

content.prompt: At 4 km per hour, how long to cover 20 km?
content.explanation: Time equals distance divided by speed: 20 divided by 4 equals 5 hours.
content.hint: Which of the three forms uses distance and speed to get time?

content.prompt: Which uses the same speed ratio correctly for a new time?

choices.text: At 5 km/h for 4 h, distance is 5 times 4 equals 20 km
At 5 km/h for 4 h, distance is 5 plus 4 equals 9 km
At 5 km/h for 4 h, distance is 5 minus 4 equals 1 km

content.explanation: Distance equals speed multiplied by time.
content.hint: Which rearrangement of speed, distance, time matches 5 km per hour for 4 hours?

lessons.title: Planning is multiplying ratios
lessons.summary: Scale and speed combine by multiplication, then a sensible check.

content.title: Two ratios meet
content.body:
To plan a day on Neverland you combine two multiplications. First, **scale**: map centimetres times km per centimetre gives ground km. Then, **time**: ground km divided by km per hour gives hours. One chain of ratios, then sense check.

- Ground = map length times scale ($km = cm \times km/cm$)
- Hours = ground divided by speed ($h = km / (km/h)$)
- Sense check: does the answer fit the daylight you have? Would a steep section slow you? Rewrite the plan, not the ground

content.prompt: Trail A is 9 cm on a 1 cm : 2 km map. At 3 km per hour, how many hours to walk it if you could hold that speed?
content.explanation: Ground is 9 times 2 equals 18 km. Time is 18 divided by 3 equals 6 hours.
content.hint: First scale, then distance divided by speed.

content.prompt: In one sentence, say why a plan that says 12 hours for a day walk needs rewriting, and name one fix.
content.answer: Twelve hours leaves no margin for rest or error, so shorten the route, choose a flatter path, or plan to camp.
content.explanation: Any sentence that notices the plan exceeds sensible daylight and proposes shortening, choosing easier terrain, or camping is good.
content.hint: Does 12 hours fit a sane daylight walk? What changes the hours?

lessons.title: Chart Neverland, then chart home
lessons.summary: Make a chart a sailor or a hiker would trust.

content.title: Two charts with ratios
content.description: On one page, chart a small Neverland: lagoon, hill, Crocodile Creek along an 8 to 10 cm winding trail, with a north arrow, a scale bar that states the ratio, and two scale computations showing ground km. On a second page, chart your own walk to a shop or park: map cm, choice of scale ratio, ground km computed, a steady speed you can hold, and hours computed, plus a one sentence sense check on whether the walk fits your afternoon. Share the ground you chose and the speed you assumed so someone could check your hours.
content.rubric:
- Neverland chart has north arrow, scale bar with ratio, and two correct ground distance computations along a winding trail
- Real walk chart shows map cm, ground km via scale, chosen speed, and hours via speed, with units
- One sense-check sentence says whether the hours fit the time available and what to change
